The unversioned latest pair it replaced had the same exposure. A floor in the manifest (refuse a release older than the installed one, or older than a pinned minimum) would make a downgrade a refusal.

hardening_notes: The deny list under the shared directory omits CLAUDE.md, output-styles and .claude.json, which an interactive `claude` session under that CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR would load as memory, output style and user-scope MCP servers (a command line per server). The bridge excludes all three and the kit runs only auth subcommands there today. But the docs give the operator a command line naming that directory, and one interactive `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=<dir> claude` would run a seat-planted MCP server unsandboxed. Denying CLAUDE.md and output-styles for write is one line each. .claude.json Claude Code must write, so either document that no session is ever run under the directory, or render it with a guard against an mcpServers key.

Blocker 1, upstream: whether a process in a dsh seat can write $DSH_HOME/profiles/thak. srt grants it, but the thak profile's file tool writes under the session cwd (a scratch directory) and the profile has no shell tool (cordis.patch.yml:13-14), so the reachable writer is the harness itself, a plugin, or a dependency. Not observed here.

Blocker 2: the threat model. The profile's lockfile is pnpm's output, written on the operator's own earlier runs, and the kit renders none. Whether the step should trust a lockfile that lies in a seat write root is the program's decision.

Proposed local plan, in the required sandbox: in a scratch DSH_HOME, write a profile lockfile with a tarball: row naming a loopback host, run update_deepseek_harness with a fake srt that records its settings, and read allowedDomains for that host, then stop.

Proposed smallest fix: derive the profile install's hosts from the kit's own state, not from a file in DSH_HOME. Either the default registry alone (the kit renders no lockfile and its plugins come from the registry), or a lockfile the kit renders and pins beside the manifest. Refuse a profile lockfile that names any other host.

(1) The Router can write the file: DSH_HOME is a write root of the router row (scripts/orchestrator/hcom-seat:2324-2327, row 3), so `$DSH_HOME/profiles/router/package.json` and `node_modules` there are Router-writable to srt. (2) The trigger: on the already-installed exit (scripts/update-agent-assets.sh:2830-2845), dsh_superagent_missing_dependencies (:2715-2725) reads every key of that file's `dependencies` (python3 -I -S, json) and prints each without a `node_modules/<name>` entry; any name re-runs the install (:2833-2842). Before U434b the profile install ran only with a new pin (the fresh-install path, same file); now a Router that adds a dependency, or removes an entry, starts it on the operator's next make update. (3) The install: build_under_srt (:2839) runs `pnpm install` (not --frozen-lockfile) in profiles/router with the registry host alone (the profile lockfile, if any, held to that host, :2835-2837), writes the profile directory and the pnpm store, and denies for read the list at :1985-1988 (credential stores, .omp/profiles, .hcom, ~/.local/state/hcom, the chezmoi dirs, Workspace, ~/.local/state/omp-seats, .claude, the checkout and its git common directory). The router row also denies every hcom store `~/.local/state/hcom-*` (dsh_deny_paths, scripts/orchestrator/hcom-seat:2510-2523) and the orchestration records; build_under_srt does not name the hcom-* stores. So a registry package the Router names, if pnpm runs its install script, can read the bus store inside the updater's sandbox and write what it read into profiles/router, which the Router reads. (4) Ordering: make update runs `chezmoi apply --verbose` (Makefile:124) before ./scripts/update-agent-assets.sh (Makefile:133); package.json is a chezmoi target (home/dot_dsh/profiles/router/package.json), so whether an edited target is restored, refused or kept before the step reads it is chezmoi's behaviour for a modified target, not source here. A missing node_modules entry alone (no edit of package.json) re-runs the kit's own dependencies, which is harmless.
